10.1016/j.atherosclerosis.2026.121960: Background and Aims Physiology-guided deferral of coronary revascularization is guideline-recommended but may overlook residual plaque vulnerability. We evaluated the prognostic value of angiography-derived radial wall strain (RWS) in coronary vessels deferred after invasive physiological assessment. Methods This blinded post-hoc analysis of a single-centre registry (NCT07186582) included vessels in which revascularization was deferred following physiological assessment. Maximum RWS (RWS max ) was derived from standard coronary angiography, with high RWS predefined as RWS max ≥13%. The primary endpoint was the vessel-oriented composite endpoint, comprising cardiac death, target vessel–related myocardial infarction, or clinically driven target vessel revascularization. Results Overall, 509 vessels from 417 patients were included. During a median follow-up of 3.3 years (IQR 1.8–6.0), the vessel-oriented composite endpoint occurred in 50 vessels (9.8%). FFR and non-hyperaemic pressure ratios did not differ between vessels with and without events, whereas RWS max was higher in vessels with events (15.4±3.9% vs 13.4±2.9%; p < 0.001). RWS max independently predicted the vessel-oriented composite endpoint (adjusted HR 1.22 per 1% increase; 95% CI 1.14–1.31; p < 0.001). RWS max ≥13% identified vessels at higher risk (HR 3.60; 95% CI 1.96–6.60; p < 0.001). RWS max showed moderate discrimination (AUC 0.69), while its addition to a clinical-physiological model increased Harrell's C-index from 0.648 to 0.732. Conclusions RWS provided incremental prognostic information beyond invasive physiology despite moderate standalone discrimination. These findings support further evaluation of RWS integrated with clinical and physiological variables to refine risk stratification and guide individualized management.
10.1016/j.atherosclerosis.2026.121966: Aims Familial hypercholesterolemia (FH) is characterized by lifelong exposure to elevated LDL-C and premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). The homozygous form (HoFH) is associated with severe aortic stenosis (AS), often requiring complex aortic valve replacement (AVR). Our aim was to conduct a systematic review (PROSPERO-CRD42024611618) to characterize the prevalence of AS and incidence of AVR in HoFH and heterozygous FH (HeFH) compared with the general population. Methods MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central, PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus and BIOSIS were searched from inception to 25 September 2025 for studies reporting AS prevalence and AVR incidence in FH and the general population. Results Among 2024 unique records identified, 53 studies met eligibility criteria. In cohorts with a mean age ≤75 years, the pooled prevalence of mild-to-severe AS was significantly higher in HoFH (32.7%; 95%CI: 26.0-40.2%; n=18 studies) and HeFH (3.4%; 95%CI: 1.5%-7.6%; n=7) compared with the general population (0.9%; 95%CI: 0.5%-1.4%; n=7) ( p <0.0001 for both comparisons). The AS prevalence was also significantly higher in HoFH than HeFH ( p <0.0001). The AVR incidence was 5.89, 1.56 and 0.18 AVR per 1,000 patient-years in HoFH, HeFH and in the general population, respectively. Conclusion A marked and graded increase in AS burden was observed across HoFH, HeFH, and the general population, with particularly high prevalence of AS and AVR rates in HoFH at relatively young ages. These findings extend the recognized cardiovascular phenotype of FH beyond ASCVD and highlight the importance of early and sustained lipid-lowering therapy to reduce LDL-C exposure and mitigate long-term valvular complications.
